question: Under the U.S. Aids to Navigation System's lateral marker numbering convention, what do the numbers on channel markers indicate?
choice_a: Numbers are assigned randomly and carry no navigational meaning
choice_b: Red markers carry even numbers and green markers carry odd numbers, with the numbers increasing consecutively as a boater heads upstream or returns from open water
choice_c: Green markers carry even numbers and red markers carry odd numbers
choice_d: Numbers decrease consecutively as a boater heads upstream or returns from open water
explanation: In the U.S. lateral marking system, red markers are always given even numbers and green markers odd numbers, and the numbers increase consecutively as a boater proceeds upstream or returns from open water into a channel.
source_note: Boat-Ed/Kalkomey Arizona boating safety course (AZGFD-approved), boat-ed.com/arizona, 'Lateral Markers: Colors and Numbers'

question: What shape is a 'nun' buoy, and what does it mark?
choice_a: A cylindrical buoy that is green with an odd number, marking the port side of the channel
choice_b: A flat, square white buoy marking an information point
choice_c: A cone-shaped buoy that is red with an even number, marking the edge of the channel on a boater's starboard (right) side when entering from open sea or heading upstream
choice_d: A striped buoy marking a swimming area closed to boats
explanation: A nun buoy is cone-shaped, colored red, and carries an even number; it marks the edge of the channel on a boater's starboard side when entering from open sea or heading upstream.
source_note: Boat-Ed/Kalkomey Arizona boating safety course (AZGFD-approved), boat-ed.com/arizona, 'Lateral Markers: Shapes'

question: What shape is a 'can' buoy, and what does it mark?
choice_a: A cone-shaped buoy that is red with an even number, marking the starboard side of the channel
choice_b: A diamond-shaped buoy warning of a hazard such as rocks or a dam
choice_c: A buoy with an orange circle marking a controlled speed zone
choice_d: A cylindrical buoy that is green with an odd number, marking the edge of the channel on a boater's port (left) side when entering from open sea or heading upstream
explanation: A can buoy is cylindrical, colored green, and carries an odd number; it marks the edge of the channel on a boater's port side when entering from open sea or heading upstream.
source_note: Boat-Ed/Kalkomey Arizona boating safety course (AZGFD-approved), boat-ed.com/arizona, 'Lateral Markers: Shapes'

question: A junction (preferred channel) marker displays both red and green horizontal bands at a point where a channel splits. How is the preferred, or primary, channel indicated?
choice_a: If the topmost band is green, the preferred channel lies to the right; if the topmost band is red, the preferred channel lies to the left
choice_b: The preferred channel is always to the right, regardless of which color band is on top
choice_c: The preferred channel is always to the left, regardless of which color band is on top
choice_d: The band colors indicate water depth, not which channel is preferred
explanation: On a junction marker with both red and green horizontal bands, the topmost color tells the boater which side holds the preferred channel: green on top means the preferred channel is to the right, and red on top means it is to the left.
source_note: Boat-Ed/Kalkomey Arizona boating safety course (AZGFD-approved), boat-ed.com/arizona, 'Lateral Markers: Colors and Numbers'

question: How do lighted buoys within the lateral marking system convey their meaning after dark?
choice_a: All lighted buoys display only a white light, regardless of the buoy's daytime color
choice_b: They display a light in the same color as the buoy itself -- a red light on a red buoy and a green light on a green buoy -- while keeping the same shape, color, and numbering meaning as their unlighted counterparts
choice_c: Lighted buoys follow a completely separate numbering system from unlighted buoys
choice_d: Lights on navigational buoys are decorative and carry no navigational meaning
explanation: Lighted buoys use the same lateral marker shapes, colors, and numbers as their unlighted counterparts, adding a matching colored light -- red on red buoys and green on green buoys -- so the meaning carries over after dark.
source_note: Boat-Ed/Kalkomey Arizona boating safety course (AZGFD-approved), boat-ed.com/arizona, 'Lateral Markers: Other Kinds of Buoys and Markers'

question: What does a white buoy with a blue horizontal band indicate, and how may a boater use it?
choice_a: It marks a hazard, such as rocks or a dam, that must never be approached
choice_b: It is a regulatory marker requiring boats to slow to idle speed
choice_c: It is a mooring buoy, typically found in marinas or designated anchorages, and it is the only type of buoy a boater may legally tie up to
choice_d: It marks a swimming area that is closed to all boat traffic
explanation: A white buoy with a blue horizontal band is a mooring buoy, usually placed in marinas or designated anchoring areas; it is the only type of buoy a boater may legally tie up to.
source_note: Boat-Ed/Kalkomey Arizona boating safety course (AZGFD-approved), boat-ed.com/arizona, 'Other Non-Lateral Markers'

question: What does a white marker with black vertical stripes indicate on inland waters, and how should a boater respond to it?
choice_a: It marks a safe, unobstructed anchorage open to all boat traffic
choice_b: It marks a fueling station or supply dock
choice_c: It indicates that the preferred channel lies to the right
choice_d: It marks an obstruction in inland waters, and a boater should not pass between the marker and the nearest shore
explanation: A white marker with black vertical stripes marks an obstruction in inland waters; a boater should not pass between the marker and the nearest shore, since the obstruction lies in that space.
source_note: Boat-Ed/Kalkomey Arizona boating safety course (AZGFD-approved), boat-ed.com/arizona, 'Other Non-Lateral Markers'

question: The 'red, right, returning' rule applies when a boater is returning from open water or heading upstream. What changes when the boater instead heads outbound, from a channel out into open water?
choice_a: The relationship reverses in most circumstances -- red markers are kept on the boater's port (left) side and green markers on the boater's starboard (right) side
choice_b: Nothing changes -- red markers are kept on the right regardless of the direction of travel
choice_c: Green markers become hazards that must be avoided entirely when heading outbound
choice_d: The numbers on the markers reverse and begin counting down when heading outbound
explanation: Because 'red, right, returning' describes travel from open water into a channel or upstream, the relationship reverses in most circumstances when a boater is instead heading from a channel out into open water: red markers are then kept to port and green markers to starboard.
source_note: Boat-Ed/Kalkomey Arizona boating safety course (AZGFD-approved), boat-ed.com/arizona, 'Lateral Markers: Red Right Returning'
